sim.title: How Sanakh decides
sim.intro: Change the schedule, the confirmations or the time of day, and watch how the algorithm detects double doses and missed doses, and when it alerts the caregiver. It uses the same rules as the real app (algorithm/rules.py). Nothing is saved.
sim.preview_note: Browser preview: a JavaScript copy of algorithm/rules.py, tested identical on 511 scenarios
sim.r1: Not confirmed within {grace} after its time (or after the allowed time, if on hold) → missed.
sim.r2: Same dose confirmed twice → blocked. Same medicine again within {gap} of its dose interval → blocked, and the dose goes on hold until the app's rule allows it.
sim.r3: On a missed dose (once), on any blocked double-dose attempt, and a follow-up if a missed dose is taken late.
sim.r4: Opens {early} before the dose time. Earlier → too early.

sim.s_gap: Minimum gap: {v} of the dose interval
sim.log_hint: Everything the algorithm did up to now, and why.

sim.p2_h: Morning dose confirmed twice → double dose blocked.
sim.p3_h: No confirmation by 20:30 → missed + alert, then taken late.
sim.p4_h: Morning dose taken at 11:20, so the 12:00 dose is too close.

tour.title: ⏱ 2-minute tour: how the algorithm works
tour.sub: 5 questions, 5 steps. Each step sets up the simulator below and shows the answer.
tour.q1: 1. When it is time for a medicine, how does the system remind?
tour.a1: From 30 min before the dose time, the dose can be confirmed. At the dose time the elder's phone shows a notification with an “I took it” button, chimes and speaks the reminder, and repeats it every 5 min until it is confirmed.
tour.q2: 2. When the user confirms “I took it”, how is it recorded?
tour.a2: The press is checked by the rules, then saved with its exact time. The database only writes it if the dose is not taken yet, so even two phones tapping at once cannot record it twice.
tour.q3: 3. When the same dose is confirmed again, how is the earlier record checked?
tour.a3: Before saving, Sanakh looks up that dose. Already taken → blocked: “You took it at 08:05”. It also checks the last confirmation of the same medicine: too soon for the app's rule → blocked until the allowed time. Both alert the caregiver.
tour.q4: 4. If a dose is not confirmed in time, how is it detected and the caregiver told?
tour.a4: Every minute the server checks each dose. Not confirmed by its time + 30 min grace → marked missed, and one Telegram alert goes to the caregiver. If it is taken later, a follow-up says so.
tour.q5: 5. When you change the time or the settings, how do the decisions change?
tour.a5: Everything is recalculated instantly from the same rules. Here the grace period is 60 min, so the evening dose pressed at 20:45 counts as on time with no alert. Drag the grace slider back to 30 min: it becomes “taken late” and an alert appears.

pv.title: Privacy
pv.intro: Sanakh keeps only what it needs to remind and to alert the family.
pv.store: The elder's and caregiver's names, medicines and times, when each dose was taken or missed, the time zone, the language and the Telegram chat ID.
pv.not: Your location, phone numbers, the PIN itself (only a scrambled hash of it), and no tracking or advertising data.
pv.who: The elder screen opens with the share code. The caregiver dashboard, history and settings also need the 6-digit PIN. Keep both private.
pv.others: Missed-dose alerts go through Telegram and include the elder's name and the medicine. The pharmacy finder sends a rounded location (about 100 m) to OpenStreetMap. Prices you add are anonymous.
pv.control: On the dashboard you can download all data, lock a device, or delete the profile and its whole history at any time.
ph.private: Your exact location stays on this phone. Only a rounded position (about 100 m) is sent to OpenStreetMap, and nothing is saved.
disc.short: 🎓 Student learning project, not a medical device. Always follow your doctor's or pharmacist's instructions.
disc.long: 🎓 Sanakh is a student learning project, not a medical device. The time gaps it uses are simple teaching rules, not medical advice. Always follow your doctor's or pharmacist's instructions, and don't rely on Sanakh as the only reminder for important medicines.
disc.sim: 🎓 Learning simulation: the minimum gap between doses is a simple teaching rule (half the time between scheduled doses), not a medical safety time. Only a doctor or pharmacist can say when a dose is safe.
idx.tour_sub: 5 short steps show how Sanakh detects double doses and missed doses, and when it alerts the family. Nothing to install.
